blocks.text: **Bubble sort** is the simplest sort to picture: walk along the array comparing **neighbours**, and swap any pair that's in the wrong order. After one pass the largest value has "bubbled" all the way to the end. Repeat until a pass makes no swaps.

blocks.alt: One pass of bubble sort over 5, 1, 4, 2, 8. Neighbours are compared left to right: 5 and 1 swap, 5 and 4 swap, 5 and 2 swap, 5 and 8 stay. After the pass the array is 1, 4, 2, 5, 8 and the largest value, 8, is in its final place at the end.

items: Compare `nums[0]` and `nums[1]`; if the left one is bigger, swap them. Move one step right and repeat to the end.
After the pass, the largest value is at the last index — its final place. The next pass can stop one step earlier.
Keep doing passes. If a pass makes **no swaps**, every neighbour is in order and the array is sorted: stop.

blocks.caption: Each step compares one pair of neighbours. Watch the sorted part grow from the right.

blocks.text: In the worst case (a reversed array) every pass swaps every pair: about n²/2 comparisons and swaps, **O(n²)**. On an already sorted array the first pass makes no swaps and the loop stops: **O(n)**. It only ever swaps neighbours in place, so the extra space is **O(1)**.

blocks.alt: Best: already sorted: O(n) time, O(1) space. Average and worst: O(n²) time, O(1) space.

items: **Stable** — it only swaps when the left value is strictly bigger, so equal values never pass each other.
**Adaptive** — with the early stop, nearly sorted input finishes in a few passes.

blocks.text: Almost never in real code — insertion sort does the same job with fewer moves. Bubble sort is worth knowing because it's the easiest sort to explain, its *one pass moves the largest to the end* idea shows up in other questions, and interviewers sometimes ask you to write it and spot its early-exit optimisation.

items: Compare and swap **neighbours**; each pass puts the largest remaining value at the end.
**O(n²)** time, **O(1)** space, **stable**; **O(n)** on sorted input with the no-swap early exit.
Each pass can stop one step earlier, because the end of the array is already sorted.
